title: Pause
tagline: Designing friction that helps people scroll on purpose.
headline: Downloads went up 170%. So why did people quit in week one?
summary: I designed, shipped and iterated a screen-time app that puts a short puzzle in front of distracting apps. Solo, with Claude Code as my engineering partner, and analytics to find where the design was losing people.
outcomes: 10+ puzzle types on one shared design system, plus seasonal themes
Downloads +170% after a metadata update, then a funnel analysis that moved the focus to week-one retention
Dead ends and onboarding drop-offs fixed; D7 gate retention 16% now, 30% is the target
lessons: AI changes the bottleneck, not the job

chapters.title: THE PROBLEM
chapters.subtitle: Screen Time is one tap to bypass

chapters.title: THE DESIGN
chapters.subtitle: Friction that feels like a pause

beats.headline: One tap to bypass
beats.body: Screen Time limits are easy to bypass by simply tapping “Ignore Limit.” Temptation hits when people are least able to enforce their own rules, so people know they're doomscrolling and do it anyway.

beats.headline: How might we…
beats.body:
…add enough friction to interrupt autopilot, without making people feel punished or locked out of their own phone?

Too little friction is a toothless timer. Too much and people delete the app.

beats.question: How much friction is the right amount?

optionA.label: Hard block
optionA.body: Lock the app behind a timer. Strong, but it feels like punishment, and people delete apps that punish them.

optionB.label: Quick puzzle
optionB.body: A short puzzle before the app opens: enough to interrupt autopilot, without locking anyone out.

beats.why: A puzzle turns the scroll into a choice.

beats.headline: One shell, many games
beats.body:
- A pause, not a punishment: warm gradients, glass, calm copy
- Varied difficulty: a speed bump for some apps, a longer slowdown for others
- One shell for every puzzle, so you learn it once
- Collect nothing I don't need

beats.caption: Friction per app: pick the difficulty

beats.headline: No more dead ends
beats.body:
The first Word Jumble trapped people after a wrong answer, right when they were already frustrated. Analytics confirmed the drop-off.

- Free retries
- Show word after a miss
- Anagrams count
- A Mix letters button

beats.question: Kill or keep the Mini Crossword?

optionA.label: Mini Crossword
optionA.body: Same clue every time, no hints. A real one needs a fill algorithm and a clue database, out of scope solo.

optionB.label: Word Search
optionB.body: A fresh 8×8 board on every gate from a calming-word list. No timer, no fail state.

beats.why: The gate fires many times a day, so a puzzle that repeats is worse than no puzzle.

beats.headline: How I work with AI
beats.body:
I own the problem, the taste and every go/no-go. Claude Code turns Figma frames into SwiftUI, audits code and analytics, and checks builds. I test everything on my phone.

AI didn't replace design judgment. It made it cheaper to act on.

beats.caption: Working alongside the emulator, with design feedback

beats.headline: The working loop
beats.body:
- Design in Figma first
- Build one thing at a time
- Test on my phone
- Write the decision down

It even caught bugs in my own analytics: puzzle_reset meant a tap on Reset, not a wrong answer.

beats.headline: Seasonal themes
beats.body: An accent layer, not a re-skin: one set of tokens for gradients, accents, fonts and decor. Halloween added Memory Match. Thanksgiving added Gratitude, where answers never leave the phone.

beats.caption: The dashboard in its Halloween theme

beats.headline: Inside platform constraints
beats.body: Screen Time keeps app names and icons as private tokens, and categories can't be expanded. Instead of hiding that, I showed app and category tiles side by side, sized the system title to match my type, and documented the rule in the code.

beats.headline: Onboarding fixes
beats.body:
Onboarding lost people at permissions and at the app picker.

- Try Again after a denied permission
- A Choose Apps screen before the picker
- Fewer, reordered steps
- A Heads up box before iOS asks
- Honest trial copy: 7 days free · Cancel anytime

beats.headline: Plot twist: week one
beats.body:
Marketing wasn't the leak. Week one was.

- D7 gate retention: 16% now, 30% is the target
- About $4.33 to get an install, about $1.14 of value per download
- Paying subscribers: still single digits
beats.note: Notion 8.4: update the results with the latest numbers once 1.7 ships (Nov 1).

beats.label: downloads after new metadata
beats.body: Impressions +137%, page views +160%. But keyword ranks stayed flat, so the lift was likely people searching for Pause by name. I stopped iterating metadata.
beats.note: Notion 8.4: update the results with the latest numbers once 1.7 ships (Nov 1).

beats.headline: Bonus: the honest numbers
beats.body:
- Impressions 775 → 1,840
- Page views 124 → 323
- Conversion 5.67% → 6.45%
- Downloads 27 → 73

Only 1 of 13 tracked keywords ranked at all, so I stopped optimising keywords.

beats.headline: Beyond the app
beats.body:
- try-pause.com, designed and built from scratch
- App Store screenshots and a preview video per season
- GA4, Search Console and comparison posts
- A roadmap page with a live vote

beats.headline: What I'd tell another designer
beats.body:
- Design the failure state first
- Systems beat screens
- Cut early
- Instrument what you design
- Stay honest with the data
- AI changes the bottleneck, not the job
